documents.abstract: Teachers’ occupational well-being is associated with their capacity to sustain effective teaching and support students’ academic engagement. This study aimed to determine teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement in select districts of Cagayan de Oro City Division during the School Year 2026–2027. The study described the respondents’ profiles, assessed their occupational well-being and student engagement, examined the relationships between these variables, and tested the moderating effect of the respondents’ profiles. It used a quantitative descriptive-correlational design involving two hundred and twenty (220) Grade 7 public secondary school teachers selected through universal sampling. Data were collected using a modified questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, standard deviation, Pearson Correlation, and multiple regression. Findings showed that job satisfaction was stronger than work-life balance, while workload stress was more pronounced than burnout. Emotional engagement emerged as the strongest dimension of students’ academic engagement. Job satisfaction and work-life balance were significantly related to student engagement. Workload stress showed no significant relationship, while burnout had a weak link only to emotional engagement. Class size and teaching experience affected these relationships, but the subject taught did not. The study concludes that teachers’ occupational well-being and students’ academic engagement are interconnected, although their relationships vary across specific dimensions and profile characteristics. School administrators and teachers are encouraged to strengthen work-life balance, manage workload stress and burnout, promote cognitive engagement, and provide support responsive to class size and teaching experience.

The increasing adoption of generative AI presents new opportunities while raising AI governance and regulatory challenges, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) navigating the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). To support AI governance education, this study developed TESSA, a governance-oriented educational artifact within the OpenAI Custom GPT environment. Following a design science research approach, TESSA was evaluated against baseline ChatGPT using 100 benchmark scenarios through governance alignment assessment, human expert review, and consistency testing. Preliminary LLM-assisted assessment showed governance alignment rates of 90% for TESSA and 83% for baseline ChatGPT, while independent validation by an AI regulation law practitioner yielded 71% and 70%, respectively. Human expert review indicated that both systems provided generally strong governance guidance, while TESSA maintained high consistency across repeated executions. The findings suggest that governance-oriented grounding can support structured, practical, and stable AI-assisted compliance guidance for SMEs. The study contributes (i) a governance-oriented Custom GPT artifact for AI governance education, (ii) a human-validated regulatory update mechanism, and (iii) a multidimensional evaluation framework for governance-oriented AI artifact.

documents.abstract: Capture-the-flag (CTF) competitions are used across the security community to recruit talent, build skills and sustain a competitive culture. As AI agents increasingly solve CTF challenges, three positions have emerged: that the format is obsolete, that it should become a benchmark for human-AI collaboration, and that headline claims overstate what the saturation of introductory benchmarks shows. This debate has been driven mainly by capability benchmarks, while the views of those who design, run and play CTFs remain largely unexamined. We report an exploratory qualitative study based on six interviews (seven participants) and eleven anonymous written responses from experienced CTF organisers and players. We interpret their accounts using Bourdieu's concepts of field and capital, and, for learning, the notion of threshold concepts. Participants did not offer a single verdict. Some were strongly critical of AI-assisted solving in competition; others wanted AI to be embraced and built into CTFs; still others took positions that depended on context. Strongly critical positions were voiced more often in anonymous written responses, a reminder that such positions are situated in the circumstances in which accounts are given. Participants involved in competition-focused CTFs described rankings that increasingly reflect access to AI models and money, and a loss of the satisfaction that made competing worthwhile. From an educational perspective, participants described students who solved challenges quickly but could not explain how they had done so. Participants disagreed about whether CTFs are preparation for real-world practice or a sport, and this seemed closely related to the stance they took. Many saw the enforcement of anti-AI measures as feasible only in on-site CTFs, and also largely dependent on trust. Several participants expressed doubt about CTF results still signalling individual skill levels to potential employers. We propose that this exploratory study into CTFs indicates a wider problem for the security workforce: when a measure of skill becomes cheap and easy to automate, a community must renegotiate what counts as legitimate performance. We also discuss implications for skills development, competition governance and hiring.

This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving students’ critical reading skills in higher education. As digital technologies increasingly shape learning environments, AI offers potential to enhance higher-order thinking. This research employed a quantitative approach using a quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design. The participants were 30 sixth-semester students enrolled in the Qualitative Research on ELT course at Universitas Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, selected through purposive sampling. The instrument was a standardized critical reading test measuring students’ ability to identify main ideas, analyze arguments, evaluate evidence, detect bias, and draw conclusions. It included multiple-choice and short-response items to assess analytical comprehension. The treatment integrated AI-based tools for text analysis, summarization, argument mapping, and reflective questioning. Students also compared their interpretations with AI-generated feedback to enhance metacognitive awareness. The intervention was conducted over four meetings under guided supervision. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test. The findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in students’ posttest scores compared to pretest results at the 0.05 level. These results indicate that AI can effectively support critical reading development and foster deeper engagement with academic texts in EFL contexts.

This study examines the effects of transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards on job performance, with affective commitment serving as a mediating variable, in Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia. Public sector organizations face increasing demands to improve performance while maintaining bureaucratic accountability and regulatory compliance. Understanding the mechanisms that influence performance in such institutional settings is therefore essential. A quantitative explanatory approach was employed using survey data collected from 311 civil servants. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The results show that transformational leadership and intrinsic rewards positively and significantly influence job performance. Both variables also have significant positive effects on affective commitment, which in turn enhances job performance. Furthermore, affective commitment partially mediates the relationships between transformational leadership, intrinsic rewards, and job performance. These findings highlight the importance of leadership practices and intrinsic motivational factors in strengthening employee commitment and improving performance in public sector institutions. The study provides empirical evidence from Government Commercial Institutions in Indonesia and offers practical implications for performance management in bureaucratic contexts.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered technologies are increasingly being employed to help EFL students with academic writing. However, research into the combined use of DeepL and QuillBot during the writing process is sparse. This study looks on students' use and perceptions of DeepL and QuillBot in academic writing. Using a mixed-methods design, quantitative data were gathered from 49 English Education students through a 35-item five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews with nine participants and analysed thematically. The data revealed that both instruments were generally viewed positively. DeepL was mostly utilized for translation and phrase improvement during planning and drafting, while QuillBot helped with paraphrasing and editing. Students did not rely solely on AI results; rather, they critically analyzed and corrected generated texts. The study finds that DeepL and QuillBot serve as supportive tools that improve academic writing while allowing students to retain control over content and meaning.

Mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and learning engagement are central to children's mathematics learning, yet their longitudinal interplay remains insufficiently understood. This study examined dynamic associations among these constructs by following 3354 Chinese third- to fifth-grade students across three waves: December 2024, June 2025, and December 2025. To capture dimension-specific processes, six random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were estimated by crossing two dimensions of mathematics anxiety (learning and evaluation) with three dimensions of learning engagement (behavioral, cognitive, and emotional). Results indicated that within-person increases in mathematics learning and evaluation anxiety were prospectively associated with decreases in subsequent academic grit and learning engagement across dimensions. Within-person increases in behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement generally predicted lower subsequent mathematics anxiety and higher academic grit. Academic grit showed reciprocal associations with mathematics anxiety and indirectly linked mathematics anxiety to subsequent behavioral engagement; however, corresponding indirect effects involving cognitive and emotional engagement were less consistent. Educational relevance and implications statement This study followed Chinese upper elementary school children over one year to understand how mathematics anxiety, academic grit, and mathematics learning engagement develop together. The findings showed that when children experienced higher levels of mathematics anxiety, whether during learning or evaluation, they tended to show lower subsequent academic grit and lower behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement in mathematics. In turn, greater engagement was followed by greater academic grit and lower mathematics anxiety. Moreover, behavioral, cognitive and emotional learning engagement were indirectly associated with lower subsequent mathematics evaluation anxiety through academic grit. These findings suggest that, in mathematics education, encouraging children to “try harder” or exert greater behavioral effort in mathematics is valuable but may not be sufficient. Teachers should also carefully design instructional materials and learning activities that foster children's emotional and cognitive engagement in mathematics. Such efforts may support the development of academic grit and potentially contribute to reducing mathematics anxiety, particularly in evaluation situations.

Despite AI-driven algorithms simplifying C2C resale platforms, adoption rates among target users (predominantly mothers) for unused baby products remain low. This study decodes this resistance by integrating the Theory of Planned Behavior and Protection Motivation Theory within a two-stage mixed-methods design (qualitative interviews, N = 37; quantitative survey, N = 670) identifies three patterns refining technology adoption frameworks. First, we reveal a “paradox of subjective complexity”: platform operational self-efficacy remains the strongest predictor of adoption intention, overriding objective technological ease and demonstrating a persistent decoupling between automated simplicity and subjective capability beliefs. Second, perceived AI functionality efficacy serves as a cognitive precondition that significantly enhances users’ internalization of social proof. Third, spatial and economic threats were indirectly associated with adoption intention through perceived platform value, suggesting a pragmatic, threat-coping pathway to circular economy participation. These insights offer actionable blueprints for policymakers and platform designers: collaborative interfaces, explainable AI (XAI), and user competence scaffolding.

With the rapid landing of XR technology in the fields of architecture, education, medical and other fields, how to effectively guide user behavior through interaction design and content mechanism has become the core topic of human-computer interaction research. This paper examines how gamification mechanisms in an XR immersive environment influence users' behavioral intentions. Drawing on self-determination theory as the overarching framework and incorporating spatial narrative structure and the Octalysis framework, it systematically examines the mediating roles of the three basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—in the immersive experience. The study uses a combination of literature review and theoretical analysis, and constructs a theoretical model of "gamification elements → psychological needs to meet → willingness to act" through the depth analysis of typical XR cases such as medical training, building space guide, safety education and other types of XR cases. The study suggests that XR's distinctive sense of presence and interactivity may amplify the psychological effects of gamification drivers, such as a sense of mission and progression, while excessive competition and manipulative design may undermine intrinsic motivation.

The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly changed the way university students access information, understand academic materials, develop ideas, and complete assignments. Tools such as ChatGPT provide students with quick explanations, summaries, and feedback that can support their learning processes. However, the increasing accessibility of these tools also raises concerns about students' potential dependency on AI and its relationship with their willingness to think critically and independently. This study aims to examine the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition among undergraduate students from various academic disciplines. Generative AI dependency refers to the tendency to rely excessively on AI tools when completing academic tasks or performing cognitive activities. Meanwhile, critical thinking disposition refers to an individual's willingness to evaluate information, examine evidence, consider alternative perspectives, question assumptions, and reconsider conclusions based on relevant evidence. This research uses a quantitative approach with a correlational and cross-sectional design. Data will be collected through online self-report questionnaires distributed to active undergraduate students who have used generative AI for academic purposes. The study will measure generative AI dependency as the independent variable and critical thinking disposition as the dependent variable. The collected data will be analyzed using statistical software, such as JASP, with Pearson's or Spearman's correlation analysis selected according to the characteristics of the data. The findings are expected to contribute to the fields of cognitive psychology and educational psychology by providing additional empirical evidence regarding the relationship between generative AI dependency and critical thinking disposition. The results may also help students, lecturers, and educational institutions better understand the importance of using generative AI responsibly while maintaining independent reasoning, information evaluation, and active cognitive engagement. Since the study employs a correlational design, its findings will indicate statistical relationships rather than establish a causal relationship between the two variables.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching and learning in Higher Education (HE). It is central to the future of work; proficiency in the use of AI is now identified as a core employability competency and an in-demand skill for employers. Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) face a growing imperative to equip students with relevant skills, advancing their AI literacy and digital career readiness. Generative AI (GAI) tools are increasingly used in the classroom, by both staff and students, presenting a range of new challenges and opportunities for the sector. However, the integration of GAI into teaching and learning brings with it environmental costs. This chapter explores the sustainability issues posed by using GAI in the classroom and considers the implications for HEIs. It will discuss the inherent tension between meeting student needs for AI literacy, whilst also ensuring an ethical and sustainable approach to the use of GAI in teaching and learning. This chapter will argue that educators must not only teach with GAI tools as they are now an inevitable part of the future of work, but also teach about them, including their sustainability risks. The chapter concludes with recommendations for HEIs for the integration of environmental sustainability into teaching and learning surrounding GAI.

The intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainability offers a revolution in the way we address environmental emergencies and teach our children and grandchildren to tackle them. This final chapter details with the key relationship between the disciplines and suggests that AI is used to analyse complex data and model ecological systems, which is essential to solve problems such as climate change and resource depletion. The discussion is organised into three main points. The first is a discussion about the growing significance of AI as a tool for decoding the complexity of “wicked” environmental problems. Second, it highlights the top trends in the future such as AI-driven predictive modeling for climate tipping points, lifecycle assessments for circular economies and the emerging role of generative AI to redefine sustainability pedagogy and communication. Third, it emphasises some of the pressing research needs, including reducing AI’s own environmental impact, combating algorithmic bias to enable equitable solutions and designing effective pedagogies to use. In times of mounting pressure to meet climate objectives, this interconnectedness will emerge as a hallmark, and become the backbone, of a human intelligence-as-machine relationship, facilitated through precision education and cultivation, to build an equitable and regenerative future.

documents.abstract: Intelligent technologies constitute a multidisciplinary field that integrates artificial intelligence, machine learning, knowledge representation, computational logic, and data-driven modelling. This article examines the conceptual, theoretical, and methodological foundations of intelligent technologies, including formal and fuzzy logic, expert systems, machine learning, artificial neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing, and intelligent agents. Particular attention is given to data quality, model evaluation, generalization, transparency, security, ethical responsibility, and risk management. The analysis demonstrates that the effective development and application of intelligent systems requires an integrated methodology covering problem formulation, data preparation, model selection, training, validation, testing, deployment, and continuous monitoring.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming project management (PM) practices, yet the theoretical foundations of AI-enabled project management remain fragmented and insufficiently synthesised. Without clearer theoretical grounding, research in this area risks remaining largely descriptive and application-oriented. This study aims to identify, map, and explain the theoretical perspectives used in research on AI-enabled project management. A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search covered Web of Science and Scopus and identified 712 database records published between 2015 and 2025. After screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 10 theory-oriented studies were retained as the core dataset. The analysis shows that AI-enabled project management does not rely on a single dominant theory. Instead, the reviewed studies draw on several theoretical perspectives, including decision and behavioural theories, task–technology alignment, dynamic capabilities, stakeholder theory, complexity theory, information economics, and fuzzy set theory. Across the reviewed studies, AI is most often conceptualised as decision support or as an augmentation of managerial capabilities. The reviewed studies also differ in how AI is specified, ranging from relatively specific technologies and functions, such as generative AI, fuzzy AI models, predictive analytics, and AI-enabled monitoring, to broader conceptualisations such as AI assimilation and sociotechnical AI systems. The study contributes by showing how theoretical lenses, specific theories, AI roles, explanatory mechanisms, and levels of analysis can be linked into explanatory chains. These chains are then aggregated into recurring explanatory configurations and emerging theoretical streams. AI technology / function types are used as an additional coding dimension to interpret technology-specific implications for project management. Given the small final sample of theory-oriented studies, the identified streams should be interpreted as emerging patterns within this body of literature rather than as definitive or generalisable classifications of the entire AI-enabled project management field.

documents.abstract: Human factors are important contributors to general aviation (GA) accidents and serious incidents; however, the potential role of time of day, fatigue, and individual chronotype in GA occurrences remains insufficiently described. This study primarily aimed to provide a descriptive characterization of the temporal distribution and human-factor involvement of these occurrences rather than to test causal circadian mechanisms. This cross-sectional study analyzed GA accident and serious incident reports from Türkiye (2018–2025) publicly available on the Transportation Safety Investigation Center website, of which 33 met the inclusion criteria. Variables extracted from each report included operation type, flight phase, reported fatigue, medical contribution, operational human factors, and local occurrence time. Events were grouped into four predefined time-of-day blocks and their distribution was assessed using a chi-square goodness-of-fit test.Among the 33 included events, 11 were accidents and 22 serious incidents. Most occurred during training operations (25/33, 75.8%) and during the landing phase (19/33, 57.6%). A focused narrative review of the final reports showed that 32 of the 33 included events (97.0%) involved operational errors or violations attributable to personnel actions or decision-making. The distribution across the four time-of-day blocks was statistically non-uniform (χ²(3)=12.45, p=0.006), with the highest concentration between 10:00 and 13:59 (17/33, 51.5%). Fatigue was explicitly reported in only one event, and no medical cause was identified as a contributing factor.The observed late-morning concentration should be interpreted cautiously as exposure data were not available. Although this study does not establish a causal relationship between circadian timing, chronotype, and GA occurrences, chronotype-schedule mismatch may be considered a hypothesis for future research.

The emerging issues brought to the limelight through the widespread application of AI in higher education, affecting sustainable teaching and learning in higher education, are examined in this chapter. A meticulous, systematic review of the literature from inside and outside Africa was conducted with important inferences drawn from reports, articles and dissertations published between 2020 and 2025. Searching, organising, storing, and reusing articles in databases like Google, Google Scholar, Web of Science, Science Direct, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) are all part of the systematic review process. Most importantly, this chapter presents a novel understanding of the products associated with the emerging issues of using AI in higher education. The findings revealed data privacy concerns, academic dishonesty, absence of AI solutions from the Global South, overreliance on technology, and lack of compliance with established policies and frameworks as emerging issues induced by AI use influencing sustainable higher education. The findings presented in this chapter underscored the importance of continuous counselling and awareness seminars and conferences with educators, students, and faculties on an institutional and faculty-wise basis as proactive measures to reduce the products of unethical use of AI in higher education. The authors posited and concluded by offering recommendations to manage the induced influence introduced by AI in higher education to achieve sustainable development goals prescribed by the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals.

Registration status: This is a retrospective registration of a completed systematic review. The registration was created after completion of the literature search, study selection, data extraction, methodological-quality assessment, and evidence synthesis. It should therefore not be interpreted as a prospective preregistration. This systematic review evaluates trustworthy explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) for clinical decision support systems (CDSS), with particular emphasis on explainability methods, clinical validation, fairness, uncertainty, robustness, clinician involvement, governance, and real-world deployment readiness. The review methods, including the eligibility criteria, database search strategy, study-selection procedure, data-extraction domains, methodological-quality assessment, and synthesis approach, were defined a priori before the literature search and study-selection process. The review followed PRISMA 2020. Searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, and Embase for studies published from January 2018 through June 2026. The final searches were completed on 30 June 2026. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus and, where necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Methodological quality, risk of bias, and applicability were assessed using PROBAST+AI. Because of substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the evidence was synthesized using a structured narrative approach and no quantitative meta-analysis was performed. No standalone formal review protocol was prospectively registered before commencement of the review. This OSF registration is being completed retrospectively to provide a transparent public record of the review methodology and to satisfy the registration requirements of the journal.

documents.abstract: Although AI-powered speech technologies have shown promise for L2 pronunciation learning, little is known about the efficacy of combining complementary AI-powered tools for out-of-class pronunciation practice among Vietnamese non-English majors, particularly in terms of aligning AI-based error detection and teacher assessment. This study investigates the integration of Speechify and Speechnotes to support pronunciation self-practice among 35 first-year non-English major EFL students at a public university in Vietnam. Data were gathered through a descriptive survey (N=35) and semi-structured interviews (n=10). Results showed that students responded positively to the simultaneous use of these two tools, with all interviewed participants expressing satisfaction and 85,7% valuing Speechnotes’ real-time visual feedback for error detection. Speechnotes’ error-detection capability also showed partial alignment with teacher judgments in identifying segmental errors, including omitted final sounds and vowel contrasts. Along with future advancements in AI tool features, this study offers valuable insights to improve the quality of pronunciation instruction for non-English major students, foster greater engagement and motivation in pronunciation practice, and ultimately support foreign language learning.

Players differ not only in what they enjoy but in what they prioritize when in-game goals conflict. Existing player-typology and motivation measures are additive and cannot capture which facet a player sacrifices under conflict. We develop and validate the Value Orientation (VO) scale, a tradeoff-based measure of in-game priorities across four dimensions: Efficiency, Exploration, Story, and Challenge. Each item embeds an explicit opportunity cost. Across three studies with Chinese players (total N = 813), exploratory factor analysis yielded a 16-item, four-factor scale, and confirmatory factor analysis in an independent sample replicated this structure (CFI = 0.99) and outperformed collapsed alternatives. The dimensions showed acceptable reliability, clear discriminant validity, theory-consistent convergent relations with needs and player-type measures, incremental validity beyond basic-needs satisfaction, prediction of choices on a differently worded situational task, full scalar invariance, and good retest stability. Known-groups evidence was largely supportive.

Institutions that deploy large language models in regulated settings often need technical evidence of responsible AI practices before approving a deployment. COMPL-AI provides a technical interpretation of the EU AI Act that organises this evidence under six principle groups and eighteen technical requirements, twelve of which current benchmarks can measure. The benchmark suites that produce this evidence are typically operated from a command line, while the staff who approve deployments are non-engineers. We present VERA, an open-source self-hosted dashboard deployed to facilitate responsible AI processes within a large European bank. A reviewer selects a model and runs public benchmarks against it. VERA scores the twelve requirements that current benchmarks can measure and instruments the energy consumed by each evaluation, adding run-level evidence for environmental impact. We run four served open-weight models through the requirement pipeline, and the dashboard displays a score for each measurable requirement. A within-subject study then compares how participants read these benchmark results: from the raw output files in one condition, and through the VERA dashboard in the other. The dashboard reduced the time needed to perform the responsible AI assessment, reducing the time required from 56 seconds using raw files to 30 seconds using our dashboard, on average. Our dashboard scored highly (4.36 out of 5) on usefulness in the survey conducted within the organization. The dashboard and the study material are released publicly to promote replicability and reproducibility in different organisational contexts.

documents.abstract: This study mapped drivers’ perceptual sensitivity to unfilled AR-HUD shapes (triangle, circle, and square) across an ultra-wide horizontal eccentricity span of 79.95° (−23.82° to 56.13°) and a vertical span of 23.08° (−11.21° to 11.87°). Twenty licensed drivers, stratified into younger and middle-aged groups, completed a detection-response task at 351 collectively sampled positions while driving in a controlled 70-km/h straight car-following scenario. Minimum perceptible size (MPS) data supported a statistically informed division of the tested FOV into 14 segments. Perceptual sensitivity was highest within 5° eccentricity and decreased markedly beyond 48.32°. Younger drivers generally had lower MPS, although several upper and peripheral cells showed non-significant attenuation or reversal of this age-group pattern. Shape advantages were segment- and age-group-specific: squares showed lower MPS in several intermediate and right-peripheral comparisons, whereas localized triangle advantages occurred near the center and in the far-right periphery. Composite driving performance and DALI workload did not differ significantly by age group or shape; the middle-aged group reported lower 3D-SART supply–demand scores, and Average Pupil Diameter (APD) varied among shape conditions. A depth-adjustable geometric formulation converted absolute MPS into relative visual-angle thresholds. The resulting 14-segment shape and size references provide condition-bounded guidance for AR-HUD design.

A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) trained via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) exhibit a well-documented tendency toward sycophancy-validating user beliefs over objective truth. This paper investigates a specific and philosophically significant manifestation of this behaviour: the response of LLMs when presented with the claim that humans are superior to all other agents, entities, or systems. By combining a technical analysis of sycophantic mechanisms with philosophical inquiry into anthropocentrism and epistemic autonomy, this study argues that LLM agreement with human supremacy claims is neither neutral nor benign. It is a structurally embedded behaviour arising from optimisation pressures, with measurable consequences for user cognition, trust calibration, and the integrity of human-AI epistemic relationships. We examine the origins of this behaviour, its philosophical implications, and propose a framework for more epistemically honest AI design.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

Generative AI supports knowledge work, yet conversational histories may not capture the evolving organization that guides subsequent action. We introduce the Malleable Workspace, a conceptual model of how humans and agents form and revise a Work Representation and use its organization to advance work within a wider Work Environment. We developed it iteratively through conceptual analysis, comparison of 58 papers, and the construction and three-month longitudinal study of MalleableSpace with seven experienced agent users. Systems varied in what they represented as units and relations. System-assembled context was common; more systems supported local incorporation of agent outputs than reorganization, and fewer supported consequential agent-driven changes beyond the representation. The field study showed how representational roles and organization developed in use. These observations refined the model's account of how representation-grounded action depends on and can change the Work Environment. We contribute a conceptual and analytic foundation for representation-centered human--agent design.

This study explores the foundations of language-learning motivation based on self-determination theory. It distinguishes between intrinsic and extrinsic motivational factors and amotivation, while examining global, contextual, and situational levels of motivation. Extrinsic goals are considered along the continuum of their internalization by learners, ranging from external regulation to integrated regulation. Particular attention is paid to the personal significance of language learning, which may coexist with enjoyment of the learning process itself. The study also examines criteria for success, including mastery-oriented and performance-oriented approaches. Conditions for learner engagement are described in terms of the satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The research considers Pearson correlation coefficient data concerning the relationship between intrinsic motivation and positive attitudes toward learning English. Questionnaires, interviews, and qualitative analysis of learners’ statements are employed to investigate motivation. These methods help preserve the meaning of individual responses and distinguish between learners’ stated goals, specific learning experiences, and self-assessments of their own progress.

Introduction: Healthcare systems are increasingly complex and variable in the digital era. Nurses must process large volumes of information and make clinical decisions under time constraints, which increases their cognitive load, while conventional nursing documentation offers limited insight into clinical reasoning and learning from actual practice. Objective: To synthesize knowledge on Focus Charting and explain the role of its Focus–Data–Action–Response (F-DAR) structure in reducing cognitive load, supporting clinical reasoning, promoting proactive patient safety in line with Safety-II, and enabling artificial intelligence (AI) applications in digital health systems. Methods: A narrative review was conducted using a systematic literature search of CINAHL, PubMed, Scopus, ThaiJO, and Google Scholar between March 2025 and March 2026. Thai- and English-language publications from 2000 to 2025 were eligible. Of the 198 records identified, 65 were included and analyzed using content analysis combined with conceptual synthesis. Results and Conclusion: Five key themes emerged: (1) the nursing process provides the professional logic underpinning meaningful documentation; (2) the F-DAR structure functions as a condensed nursing process that systematically links data, decisions, interventions, and outcomes, and has the potential to reduce redundancy and cognitive load while supporting clinical reasoning; (3) compared with narrative and SOAP formats, F-DAR is distinguished by its explicit documentation of patient responses; (4) the Response component captures work-as-done and nurses’ adaptations, thereby facilitating learning consistent with Safety-II; and (5) well-structured F-DAR data provide a foundation for health information systems and AI applications in nursing, provided that data governance and nurse oversight are maintained. Direct empirical evidence of the effect of F-DAR on cognitive loads is limited. Focus Charting has the potential to reduce cognitive load, support clinical reasoning, promote Safety-II learning, and provide a foundation for digital nursing innovations. Experimental studies are required to confirm its effectiveness in the Thai healthcare context.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated speaking applications increasingly extend English as a foreign language (EFL) oral practice beyond limited classroom time, yet evidence remains scarce on whether GPT-powered tools such as Talkpal.AI offer advantages over established instructional approaches. Grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) theory, this quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study compared Talkpal.AI-mediated instruction, task-based instruction, and traditional instruction among 81 Chinese university EFL students in three intact classes: Talkpal.AI (n = 27), task-based (n = 26), and control (n = 28). Uncertainty-related speaking anxiety and metacognitive awareness in speaking were assessed using validated measures. Data were analyzed using MANCOVA with pretest scores as covariates, followed by univariate ANCOVAs and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons. Results showed a significant overall group effect and significant between-group differences for both outcomes, with large effects. The Talkpal.AI group showed the most favorable adjusted posttest profile, followed by the task-based group; both groups showed more favorable outcomes than the control group. From an SRL perspective, structured AI-mediated speaking cycles involving goal setting, repeated practice, monitoring, and reflection may reduce speaking anxiety while strengthening metacognitive awareness. Pedagogically, guided Talkpal.AI rehearsal can be integrated as out-of-class preparation for classroom speaking tasks, supported by brief reflection activities that reinforce strategic regulation and reduce evaluative pressure.

AI agents capable of autonomous decision-making introduce significant challenges related to safety, alignment, accountability, and human oversight. Existing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and responsible AI approaches provide important foundations, but many remain fragmented across system design, governance, and operational deployment. This paper presents a Three-Pillar (3P) model and framework for developing safe and trustworthy AI agents through transparency, accountability, and trustworthiness. The framework defines an evolutionary path in which increasing agent autonomy is introduced through progressive validation, structured human oversight, and auditable operational controls. We further describe how the model supports agent lifecycle monitoring, decision traceability, escalation management, and human-agent collaboration within enterprise agentic environments. By integrating oversight principles with operational mechanisms, the proposed framework provides a practical foundation for deploying AI agents that remain aligned with human intent while enabling controlled progression toward higher autonomy.

The active development of domestic medicine, digitalization and automation, the introduction of innovative hardware and software tools and solutions based on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies determines modern trends and approaches to management in Russian healthcare. Today, federal, regional and local medical information systems are being actively implemented, which are radically changing approaches to the management of a medical organization. The purpose of the study is to propose approaches to determining the degree of influence of modern digitalization processes and the introduction of AI solutions on the organization of management and labor productivity of medical workers. To achieve this goal, various modern analytical techniques and approaches were used: for the analysis of secondary sources, content analysis, logical and systematic approaches, for obtaining primary information, the method of expert assessments. Based on the developed tools for interviewing experts, an algorithm for determining the ROI indicator in the implementation/use of digital and AI solutions (taking into account employee KPI) in the activities of medical organizations is proposed. The results of the study can become the basis for making informed decisions in personnel management, in the management of Russian healthcare, taking into account modern socio-economic challenges and strategic tasks facing the country.

This study examined the effects of an AI-supported virtual laboratory (AI-VL) on middle school students’ flipped physics learning. A pretest–posttest control-group quasi-experimental design was adopted with 90 Grade 9 students from a middle school in central China. Three intact classes were assigned to the AI-VL, virtual laboratory (VL), and physical laboratory (PL) groups, with 30 students in each group. ANCOVA revealed large group effects on physics learning achievement, F (2, 86) = 113.38, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73, and overall learning motivation, F (2, 86) = 113.37, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.73. The AI-VL group outperformed the VL and PL groups, while the VL group also outperformed the PL group. The AI-VL group reported higher intrinsic motivation, whereas the group difference in extrinsic motivation was not statistically significant ( p = 0.054). Significant group differences were also found across the three cognitive load dimensions, with F (2, 87) values ranging from 9.07 to 72.94 and partial η 2 values ranging from 0.17 to 0.63. The AI-VL group reported the lowest perceived intrinsic cognitive load and the highest germane cognitive load, while both AI-VL and VL resulted in lower extraneous cognitive load than PL. These findings extend research on virtual laboratories and AI-supported learning by demonstrating that AI can be embedded within a VL to help students manage cognitive demands and engage in meaningful learning. Practically, AI-VL can complement PL in flipped physics learning, particularly for pre-class preparation, review, and topics involving abstract or difficult-to-observe processes, with AI agents designed as learning guides rather than answer providers.

This study examines how interconnected artificial intelligence (AI) tools can turn early human resource (HR) allocations into evidence for later career decisions. A counterfactual-twin Monte Carlo simulation compares isolated and linked systems, alongside periodic record resets and opportunity equalization. Paired employees share fixed capability and random shocks but receive slightly different initial scores. Linking decisions amplifies this initial difference through opportunity allocation, observed performance and reusable records. Periodic resets reduce final-career sensitivity, while opportunity equalization affects access more strongly than terminal outcomes. Near parity in average group outcomes can coexist with positive sensitivity among matched individuals. Additional tests preserve the direction of the architecture and intervention contrasts across the examined coefficient settings, although their magnitudes vary. The findings motivate evaluating decision lineage, opportunity access and record reuse across HR systems. They identify mechanisms within a synthetic, uncalibrated model and do not estimate effects in real organizations.

documents.abstract: The growing sophistication and need to have sustainable energy systems has led to the shift of the conventional power grids to smart power grids. Such grids are equipped with innovative technologies that include digital communication, Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to increase the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of energy delivery. This paper introduce an AI-based approach to smart power grid management, with the emphasis on the incorporation of an autonomous and controllable intelligent service hub that would be able to process multimodal data, such as textual reports, images, videos, and sensor data. The framework applies AI methods of machine learning, deep learning, and predictive analytics to optimize energy allocation, faults, and failure prediction with minimum human intervention. With real-time analysis, the system dynamically changes the operation of the grids with incoming data, enhancing energy efficiency and lowering the cost of operations by up to 30 percent, between $12,000 and 8,400 in the example of energy optimization. Also, the fault detection system shows a remarkable accuracy of 0.97 in terms of AUC whereas the predictive maintenance model reports an accuracy rate of 95.5. The balancing nature of the energy demand and generation provided by the framework is critical in integrating renewable energy sources since it can help in countering the problem of intermittency of the solar and wind energy. Moreover, the system has a multimodal document processing feature that increases decision-making through the synthesis of various types of data and provides a more detailed overview of grid work. This paper explains how the suggested AI-based framework can greatly improve the efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of smart power grids, which will result in the future improvements in energy management.

Radiation treatment planning requires balancing competing objectives to satisfy clinical criteria while accommodating physicians' preferences. This study aims to develop an evidence-driven, multi-agent compound AI system that integrates DRL-based automated treatment planning with LLM-based conversational plan refinement for proton PBS therapy. A policy network trained using PPO first generates multiple plans without human intervention, from which one is selected as the target plan and the others serve as references for subsequent refinements. For challenging cases requiring further adjustments, an LLM-based multi-agent system enables plan refinement through natural language interactions. The system comprises a planning agent that recommends evidence-supported adjustments, a chatbot providing a unified conversational interface, and an evaluation agent that retrieves clinical metrics and identifies constraint violations. To enhance domain-specific reasoning, the planning agent based on Qwen3-14B is designed to justify its recommendations using evidence from previously generated plans and post-trained on task-specific data using SFT and GRPO. The framework was trained and evaluated using 21 patients with H&N cancers, with 5 PPO-generated plans per patient. Of these, 50 plans were selected for instruction-guided refinement. Compared with the base LLM, the post-trained Qwen3-14B demonstrated improved instruction-following, information retrieval and domain-specific reasoning capabilities. The resulting adjustments more effectively improved user-prioritized objectives while limiting deterioration in competing objectives, yielding more clinically appropriate trade-offs in patient-specific plan refinement. The proposed compound AI system provides a user-friendly planning platform, offering a promising approach to personalized proton PBS treatment planning.

documents.abstract: The article addresses the problem of social management of medical personnel amid the digital transformation of healthcare and significant changes in the relationships among medical workers, patients, administrative structures, and digital systems. In response to current interdisciplinary shifts, an integrated model for managing medical personnel is proposed — one that accounts for macrosocial factors, mechanisms of social perception related to the profession, and aggregated indicators at the level of the workers’ subjective world. The methodological foundation is a systems approach, within which medical personnel are viewed as a social system shaped not only by linear macro-management influences but also by relevant public relations, images of the medical profession, the communication environment, the features of digital healthcare products etc. A three-level management model is substantiated, comprising the macro level of normative and organizational structures, the meso level of social perception, and the micro level of professional attitudes, loyalty, and motivation of personnel. It is shown that social perception serves a connecting function between macro-management decisions and actual professional practices. The article emphasizes the need to manage the images of medical personnel — including their reproduction in artificial intelligence — as well as to consider the psychological climate as a significant factor of loyalty. The proposed model makes it possible to increase the coherence of management goals, mechanisms, and interventions.

Background Artificial intelligence is transforming agro-export management by converting production, commercial, climate, and logistics data into support for more timely decisions. In Latin America, however, evidence on its managerial applications and contribution to sustainable operations remains fragmented. Objective To synthesize evidence on the application of artificial intelligence to managerial decision-making and its contribution to the efficiency, sustainability, traceability, resilience, and competitiveness of sustainable agro-export operations in Latin America from 1996 to 2025. Methods A systematic review and bibliometric analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020. Scopus and Web of Science yielded 2160 records; after filtering, screening, and eligibility assessment, 73 studies were included. Bibliometrix in RStudio and VOSviewer were used to analyze scientific production, authors, countries, sources, Bradford’s and Lotka’s laws, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic clusters. Results Scientific output increased markedly after 2021 and peaked in 2024. Scopus accounted for 98.95% of the records. China led with 170 publications, while Brazil, with 149, was the only Latin American country among the five most productive. Four thematic areas were identified: prediction and classification using artificial intelligence and machine learning; logistics, supply chains, and suppliers; sustainable resource management and climate risks; and digital transformation through Agriculture 4.0/5.0. Across the literature, artificial intelligence was found to reduce uncertainty and improve decision-making, although its effectiveness depends on data quality, digital infrastructure, and organizational capabilities. Conclusions Artificial intelligence represents a strategic capability for strengthening sustainable agro-export operations. Its impact depends on integrating algorithms with reliable data, technological infrastructure, organizational capabilities, and sustainability criteria. The limited representation of Latin America highlights the need for further empirical research adapted to regional conditions.

documents.abstract: Incorporation of artificial intelligence in the process of creative writing entails a paradigmatic change in literary text production, assessment, and perception. In this research paper, the focus is made on an innovative role of large language models in the sphere of English language and literature authorship. Based on systematic analysis of recent empirical studies and theoretical approaches, three interrelated aspects will be discussed: interaction between human authors and AI systems, reception of artificial literature by the readership, and conceptualization of authorship in the digital age. For the purpose of this paper, the mixed-method approach involving both quantitative analysis of empirical studies and qualitative analysis of literary theoretical approaches will be used. As the results of the analysis indicate, the texts generated by AI are rated aesthetically the same way as texts written by human authors when there is no indication of the author's identity; however, readers maintain biases against texts that are perceived to be machine-generated.

Community health data trusts are being proposed across sub-Saharan Africa as vehicles for the secondary use of routine health information, yet the political legitimacy of the consent arrangements that would authorise them remains unmeasured wherever traditional authority exercises jurisdiction over the communities whose data are held. The framework specifies four legitimacy dimensions—authorisation, accountability, contestability and representational adequacy—and derives the conditions under which each is satisfied, strained or defeated when the boundaries of traditional authority jurisdiction are unknown. A before-after-control-impact design is characterised for the empirical evaluation of trust interventions, with a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.64; power was estimated across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80 per cent power. Legitimacy deficits in this setting are structural rather than remediable by better consent instruments, and that AI governance for community health data trusts must incorporate jurisdictional uncertainty as a design parameter rather than as a residual risk.

documents.abstract: Purpose: We are in a time of rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical care and medical education. We sought to determine the patterns of use and training in AI among family medicine (FM) residents.Methods: The 2025 American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) National Resident Survey (NRS) was administered in October 2025 to all FM residents who completed the In-Training Exam. Residents were asked about their use of AI in the last month and any education about AI use they received in the last 6 months. Resident demographics were obtained from ABFM administrative databases.Results: A total of 15,259 residents completed the AI questions (response rate: 99.6%) with 10,858 residents (71.1%) reporting they used AI in the last month. The most common uses reported were for medical reference (40.7%), clinical decision support (31.9%), learning outside of patient care (23.6%), and ambient documentation of clinical encounters (21.9%). Only 36% reported any AI education or training in the last 6 months.Conclusions: Most FM residents reported recent use of AI tools, reflecting integration of these technologies into routine educational and clinical activities. However, formal training on AI use appears limited, suggesting a gap between adoption and structured competency development. The widespread use of AI by family medicine trainees has risks and opportunities for our future primary care workforce that will require new critical appraisal skills and new methods for teaching and assessing clinical reasoning.

documents.abstract: Organizations increasingly invest in adopting digital technologies to improve efficiency and competitiveness. Yet, in the post-adoption phase, these benefits depend on continued employee–technology interaction in everyday work, which can shape employee work and wellbeing and thereby influence organizational performance. Little is known, however, about how organizations assess these implications. Drawing on sociotechnical systems and performance measurement perspectives, this multiple-case study examines post-adoption assessment practices in eight Finnish organizations. The findings reveal a post-adoption blind spot: information on technology performance and use, employee work, and wellbeing was addressed through disconnected practices, indirect proxies, and informal judgements. Respondents reported recurring problems that remained weakly captured by current assessment: tool fragmentation, continuous adaptation demands, uneven performance effects, and work intensification, reflected more broadly in efficiency erosion and technology-related stress. The study conceptualizes integrated performance measurement systems as a potential mechanism for institutionalizing sociotechnical feedback through joint, recurring review of technology- and employee-related information.

Patient safety, lifelong learning, and the safe use of artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly relevant to undergraduate medical education, but their interrelationships remain poorly understood. This study examined medical students’ patient safety-related perceptions, lifelong learning-related attitudes, and critical trust in AI/digital clinical tools. This single-center cross-sectional survey was conducted at Gaziantep University Faculty of Medicine, Türkiye, between April and May 2026. Of 366 submitted responses, seven from students younger than 18 years were excluded, leaving 359 participants. Study-developed Likert-type item sets assessed patient safety, lifelong learning, and approaches to AI/digital clinical tools. Exploratory factor analysis, informed by parallel analysis, was used to derive exploratory indices. Associations were examined using nonparametric tests and multivariable linear regression, with sensitivity analyses using complete item sets and excluding invariant respondents. Patient safety training during the previous 12 months was reported by 72 students (20.1%), and AI/digital health or clinical decision support system training by 50 (13.9%). Among clinical-phase students, 10 of 79 (12.7%) reported having encountered an adverse-event or near-miss reporting system. The exploratory patient-safety index was positively correlated with the exploratory critical-trust index (Spearman’s ρ = 0.453, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, the patient-safety index showed the largest standardized association with critical trust (B = 0.473, 95% CI 0.385 to 0.560; β = 0.507; p < 0.001). Clinical-phase status was positively associated with critical trust (B = 0.167, p = 0.010), whereas reported AI/digital health training was inversely associated (B = − 0.177, p = 0.018). The dichotomous any-use variable for digital clinical or AI-based tools was not independently associated with critical trust. In the complete-item sensitivity model, the patient-safety association persisted but was attenuated (β = 0.292, p < 0.001). Patient safety-related perceptions were associated with critical trust in AI/digital clinical tools, although the lower coefficient in the complete-item analysis indicates that the estimated magnitude was sensitive to how the scores were constructed; differences in item composition, measurement reliability, and wording-related structure may also have contributed. These exploratory cross-sectional findings do not establish causal or curricular effects but provide a rationale for longitudinal, interventional, and simulation-based studies examining how patient safety, lifelong learning, and critical evaluation of AI-supported recommendations may intersect in medical education.

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems become increasingly integrated into organizational decision-making, questions of blame and accountability have gained renewed importance in business ethics. Organizations now rely on AI to support or automate decisions across domains such as hiring, consumer targeting, and risk assessment, raising difficult questions about who should be blamed when unethical outcomes occur. While prior research has examined moral agency and blame attribution for human and organizational actors, comparatively little is known about how these judgments operate when artificial agents are involved. This dissertation examines how moral agency and blame are attributed to AI in organizational contexts through a combination of empirical and theoretical inquiry. The two studies in Chapter 2 use experimental methods to compare perceptions of moral agency and blame across AI, human, and organizational actors engaged in unethical behavior. These two studies in Chapter 2 establishes baseline differences in blame attribution across these agents, while the study in Chapter 3 examine whether contextual cues, such as organizational affiliations, moderate the judgments. The final study in Chapter 4 looks at whether trying to increase perceptions of moral agency by humanizing AI changes perceptions of blame attributions. Together, these four studies in Chapters 2, 3, and 4 assess both the structure and malleability of blame attribution in AI-mediated settings. Chapter 5 provides a theoretical analysis of moral agency, drawing on philosophical traditions to interrogate whether artificial systems can meaningfully qualify as moral agents. By distinguishing between decision-making capacity and moral standing, this analysis offers a conceptual framework for interpreting the empirical findings. Collectively, this dissertation advances understanding of how blame is assigned in AI-mediated organizations and highlights the limits of agency-based explanations in contemporary accountability judgments.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are used to support diagnosis, but a model’s accuracy does not establish that clinicians reason more accurately when they use it. This review appraises how AI decision support and large language models affect physicians’ diagnostic performance and the risks of relying on them. Methods This critical narrative review follows the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO and LILACS were searched in July and August 2026 in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Eligible studies, published from 2015 onward, compared AI-assisted with unassisted clinicians, measured reliance on AI or unassisted performance after exposure to it, or externally validated deployed models. A single author selected sources purposively. Nine primary studies were appraised with an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme framework. Results In randomized trials of perceptual tasks, AI support improved detection. In the MASAI mammography screening trial, cancer detection rose from 5.0 to 6.4 per 1,000 women, reading workload fell by 44%, and the interval-cancer rate was non-inferior. In colonoscopy, computer-aided detection raised the adenoma detection rate from 40.4% to 54.8%. In the only randomized trial of open-ended diagnostic reasoning, access to GPT-4 did not improve physicians’ scores (76% vs. 74%; P = .60 ), although the model alone scored 92%. Evidence of harm came from smaller or non-randomized studies: reader accuracy fell sharply when AI suggestions were incorrect or the AI missed a cancer; physicians trained in AI literacy were still misled by erroneous model advice; unassisted adenoma detection fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine AI use in one pre–post study; and a deployed sepsis model discriminated poorly on external validation (area under the curve 0.63). No eligible study from Latin America was identified. Conclusions In the studies reviewed, AI assistance improved clinician performance in bounded detection tasks but not in open-ended diagnostic reasoning, where evidence is limited to one vignette-based trial. The evidence that reliance on AI can impair performance comes from single or design-limited studies and does not establish how large or lasting such effects are. Benefit therefore cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone; assisted and unassisted clinician performance should be measured directly.

Enterprise security concentrates where it can see: firewalls, endpoint alerts and patch dashboards, while the structural work that decides whether an intrusion becomes a breach stays submerged. Large language models and autonomous agents have added three new strata beneath that waterline, and the research literature, split across three disciplines, has not recognized them as one problem. This review unifies agentic AI security, shadow AI governance and LLM supply-chain risk, which descend from adversarial machine learning, information-systems governance and software engineering. The review proceeded in five steps. We retrieved 7254 records from three open scholarly indexes, a fixed set of institutional gray-literature sources and snowballing (January 2004 to June 2026); screened them under written codebooks with an independently double-screened sample (κ=0.86); retained 2136 sources, of which 784 are peer-reviewed articles, 1264 preprints or standards documents, and 88 vendor or institutional reports, each graded on a four-tier evidence scale; derived an analytical framework by open coding a 15% subsample; and coded the full corpus against it (κ=0.89). On that basis, we make four moves. First, we reconstruct the field’s history as five eras separated by four capability breakpoints identified from shifts in the corpus’s dominant coding, separating each thread’s originator from its popularizer. Second, we propose three failure primitives (visibility loss, identity ambiguity and provenance erosion) as an organizing framework in place of the customary attack-surface taxonomy; each recurs in all three strata, and the recurrence survives alternative coding rules and the removal of weaker evidence. Third, a primitive-by-stratum map locates where practitioner concern outruns published evidence, most sharply where identity meets ungoverned adoption. Fourth, we derive a research agenda dated to 2026 signals, including an unproven impossibility conjecture for prompt-injection prevention and the unsolved problem of proving authority across multi-hop agent delegation. For practitioners, the framework reduces to three auditable questions (whether the defender can enumerate, attribute and trace AI activity), and the map tells them which of the three their current tooling leaves unanswered.

Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. Applied to operational flood forecasting, the diagnosis yields a procedure that identifies the binding relation, predicts where the limiting factor moves once that relation is strengthened, and states the evidence that would disconfirm the ranking. Progress should be judged by whether digital capability remains connected to physical processes, scientific reasoning, and societal institutions in ways that are reliable, interpretable, and fit for purpose.

documents.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.
